request.command: python3 bench/spec_replay.py bench/results/2026-10-12/m1-ngram/replay B greedy --spec-type ngram-cache
request.report:
A/greedy run finished (exit 0, ~13 min). I analyzed off vs A and chose B = `--spec-type ngram-cache` (a different ngram mechanism, not a retune of ngram-mod), and recorded the results + justification in bench/m1-notes.md §9 (restored §8 which I had accidentally clobbered, then re-appended §9 cleanly).

Foreground decode tok/s (sum(predicted_n)/sum(predicted_ms)):
- single-agent: off 55.1 | A 86.0 (draft_n 8229, acc 6212, 0.755)
- single-mem: off 55.6 | A 53.1 (draft 740, acc 69, 0.093)
- dual-agent: off 26.3 | A 25.5 (draft 1856, acc 259, 0.140)
- dual-mem: off 25.0 | A 23.8 (draft 740, acc 69, 0.093)

Read: ngram-mod helps single-slot agent a lot (+31 tok/s, 75.5% acceptance) but does NOT help with both slots busy — dual-agent and dual-mem are slightly worse. That already argues against the deploy rule. Spec also inflates capped outputs (length finishes: off single-agent 1 -> A 3; dual-agent 0 -> 2), so I'll report dual speedups with and without length.

Why B=ngram-cache: isolates whether the dual weakness is ngram-mod-specific or intrinsic to ngram speculation, and matches the traffic regime (large prefix-cache hits). If B also fails on dual, the no-deploy conclusion is robust.

Next session: read B results, pick best(A vs B) for dual, then run prod for off and best.
request.why: Config B (ngram-cache, a second distinct ngram type vs ngram-mod), greedy replay, 4 phases on fresh servers at :8089 with production flags. Tests whether A's dual-slot weakness is ngram-mod-specific or intrinsic to ngram speculation, per bench/m1-notes.md §9.
